THE MOMENT: Rush hour has stopped dead on a Tokyo avenue, humid summer evening, the sun just gone behind the buildings.

COMPOSITION -- never centred, always angled: A wide general view of the street, taking in buildings, trees and signage as much as the traffic. The camera stands well off to one side of the road, not on its centreline, turned obliquely so the avenue runs away diagonally, the vanishing point pushed far off to one side. Strictly no symmetry: no centred one-point perspective, no vanishing point in the middle, no mirrored left and right, never looking straight down the road. The left-hand buildings tower and take more width. Camera at roughly head height, the traffic seen from a shallow angle, the city filling the upper half of frame.

THE JAM -- solid, no gaps: The road is choked with stationary vehicles filling the entire road surface, bumper to bumper and side by side, right up against the kerb on both sides. No empty lane, no clear channel, no gap beside either kerb, no open strip of asphalt anywhere a vehicle could drive. No median, crash barrier, railing or divider splits the road. Only thin slivers of wet asphalt show between bumpers.

EVERY VEHICLE FACES THE CAMERA: Without exception every vehicle on the road points toward the lens, showing its front -- grilles, bumpers, plates, bonnets, windscreens, headlamps. We never see a boot, tailgate, rear window, rear bumper or red tail-light, not one, anywhere, including the vehicles nearest the kerbs. None turned away, none side-on, none parked or pulled over at the kerb.

IRREGULAR, NOT REGIMENTED: The jam is alive and untidy, never a tidy grid. Most vehicles sit roughly straight but many are askew -- some turned a couple of degrees left, others right, some crept forward out of line, others hanging back, noses at different distances. Lanes bunch and drift, gaps between bumpers vary, rows broken and staggered. Nothing lines up perfectly, nothing is evenly spaced.

VARIETY -- every vehicle different: A mixed period Tokyo jam. Several bright red cars scattered through it, crimson taxis, plus mustard-gold, cream-and-red, ivory, deep green, black and dull silver. Bodies of different shapes and sizes jumbled together: boxy saloon taxis, a tall white box truck, a cream high-roof minivan, a small kei van, a low compact hatchback, a delivery van. Taller bodies break the roofline so the top edge of the traffic rises and falls unevenly.

THE HEADLAMPS -- all lit: Every vehicle has both headlamps burning, from the nearest bumper to the smallest dot in the distance. Not one dark front. Each lamp blows to clipped white at its centre with a warm amber rim and a soft halo, the nearest flaring into wide discs, those behind shrinking to hot white points. Each pair drags a smear of light down the wet asphalt.

THE CITY -- as much as the traffic: Buildings rise on both sides, jostling heights, pale olive-grey concrete and tile. Along the left, tall narrow signboards pile up in an overlapping crush, jutting at different angles, dense with characters. Neon boards switched on down both sides, glowing from within in scarlet, amber, jade-green, white and blue -- a dense constellation into the distance. Full leafy green street trees line both pavements, dark and dusty, breaking the facades. Streetlamps, a blue direction sign, pedestrians small on the pavements.

THE FLYOVER: A single concrete expressway crosses the avenue in the far middle distance, small in frame and high up, set at an oblique angle rather than square across -- it need not be perpendicular. Its deck is jammed too, vehicles in profile along the parapet against the pale sky. Only one, no second bridge.

LIGHT: The sky above the rooftops is blown to pale warm cream, the brightest thing in frame. Where the silhouettes meet it, a burning amber-orange line ignites along every roofline and antenna. The topmost floors catch the last raking gold; all below has fallen into shade. Haze is clear in the foreground, thickening with distance until the far street pales to cream.

GRADE: Warm golden sunset light over an olive-green city. Warmth is confined to the sky, the lit signs, the glowing bodywork of the cars and the foreground asphalt, which catches a rich amber bounce. Everything else is olive khaki-green, faintly cool -- concrete, shaded shopfronts, the deep green of the trees -- never golden, never neutral, never blue. Reds and golds on the cars stay fully saturated. No black in the metal: the darkest tone is saturated russet-brown. Blacks lifted. Strong halation around the sky line, neon and headlamps.

CAMERA & LENS: Arriflex 535B on a vintage uncoated telephoto prime, wide open, light black diffusion. The nearest cars stay sharp, the street beyond falling into soft blur. Fine soft 35mm grain, a hazy glowing rendering, not crisp digital.

FEELING: A city holding its breath in the heat, going nowhere, lit like a carnival.

empty. Nobody there.

THE ROAD: a single narrow ribbon of concrete carriageway, no more than four lanes, winding and
curving away from the camera — bending left, then right, then left again — climbing and falling in
long shallow arcs, running on and on until it disappears over the horizon. It has no beginning and
no end. Steel crash barriers down both sides, dented and unpainted. Faded white lane markings.
Cracked expansion joints. Concrete pillars descending from beneath it into nothing.

THE VOID BELOW: on both sides of the road, beyond the barriers, absolute darkness. No city, no
lights, no ground, no water, no bottom — the road is simply suspended in black. Nothing visible
below or beside it.

THE MOON: an enormous moon low on the horizon behind the road, filling a large part of the sky,
its craters and maria clearly visible, pale silver-green. It is by far the brightest thing in the
picture, and the expressway runs directly toward it, the road ahead silhouetted against its disc.

THE LAMPS: a line of tall sodium street lamps marching down one side of the road, curving over it,
receding into the distance and following the curves. Their light is warm amber, small pools falling
straight down onto the concrete, pool after pool into the depth, the gaps between them longer than
the pools. A few are dead and dark.

A TRAFFIC LIGHT: standing alone at the near end of the road, a single ordinary traffic signal on a
steel post, absurd out here, its red lamp lit — one small brick-red point against the vast empty
road.

LIGHT: cool pale moonlight from behind and above, silhouetting everything and rimming the barriers
and the concrete edges. Warm sodium raking in from the side. Nothing else.

COLOUR: Kodak film stock look, warm restrained palette limited to olive green, khaki, amber,
tungsten gold, ochre, mustard yellow, brick red and terracotta against warm greys and cream.

no magenta, no electric blue. Saturation rationed, one saturated object per frame.

the sodium lamps and the moon, heavy visible organic grain heaviest in the shadows. Slightly faded
vintage film feel.

Photorealistic 35mm film photograph. Costume reference plate, three views of the same figure
arranged left to right across one sheet in this exact order: first the full length front view,
second the full length reverse view, third a tight head shot filling the entire remaining third
of the sheet. All three on the same empty seamless neutral mid grey studio backdrop, same neutral
lighting, same lens. No frame, no border, no film edge, no sprocket holes, no lettering anywhere.

THE MAN
A 20-year-old Japanese man, a pizza delivery courier. Thin and slight, narrow shoulders, long
neck, standing straight with arms hanging loose at his sides. Plain, unremarkable, faintly
awkward. Looking straight at the camera.

FACE
Narrow face, warm skin with visible pores and natural uneven tone, faint sheen on the nose and
forehead. Wide dark brown eyes, alert and slightly startled. Straight dark eyebrows, the left one
marginally higher. Ears that stick out noticeably from the sides of his head, standing away at a
clear angle, fully exposed by his short hair, catching a little light through the rims. A small
dark mole on the left cheek and another beside the nose. Small mouth, lips slightly parted.
Asymmetrical features, one eye a little smaller than the other. No stubble.

GLASSES
Large round glasses with thin pale gold wire frames, slightly too big for his face, sitting a
little crooked. Fine wire bridge with a twist of repair wire wrapped around it. One lens carries a
long fine scratch. Smudged.

HELMET — WORN IN ALL THREE VIEWS, INCLUDING THE HEAD SHOT
A cheap open-face half helmet, worn on his head in every view without exception. Cream white shell
gone yellowish with age, paint crazed with fine cracks, grubby with grey grime, rusted rivets
around the rim, black scrape marks across the shell. Covered in faded stickers applied crookedly
and overlapping: a retro tin robot, a green cartoon dinosaur, two circular racing roundels in red
and blue, one sticker half peeled leaving a pale ghost. A navy blue woven fabric chin strap,
frayed with loose threads, fastened under his chin with a worn metal buckle.

HAIR — SHORT, WILD AND FLAT, PUSHED OUT SIDEWAYS BY THE HELMET
Black, thick, cut short and badly, pressed flat under the helmet and forced outward in short spiky
tufts all around its rim — over the forehead, at both temples, in front of the ears, and at the
nape. The tufts are stubby and stick out sideways rather than hanging down; nothing reaches his
collar and nothing covers his ears. Nothing stands up on top; the helmet holds it down. Messy,
greasy, roughly cut.

GLOVES
Worn fingerless riding gloves in faded brown leather, the fingers cut off at the first knuckle so
his bare fingertips show. Cheap imitation racing gloves — moulded protective plates over the
knuckles and short ridged guards along the backs of the hands, the kind sold to look like proper
racing kit and never close to it. The leather is scuffed pale at the knuckles and creased deep
across the palms, the cut edges of the finger openings frayed and curling, the wrist closure
losing its grip, the plates scratched and one of them cracked. Grubby, softened, shaped by years
of use.

JACKET — YELLOW DELIVERY UNIFORM, ENORMOUSLY OVERSIZED, STIFF FABRIC
A bright warm yellow courier delivery uniform jacket, issued workwear, hugely oversized on him,
easily four or five sizes too big, hanging off his thin frame like a tent. Made of stiff heavy
technical fabric that holds its own shape rather than draping — the panels stand out from his
body, the collar stands upright on its own, the hem holds a rigid rectangular line, sharp creases
stay where they fold. Worn open with the zip fully undone.
The shoulder seams drop halfway down his upper arms. The sleeves are far too long and are rolled
back on themselves into thick stiff cuffs at the wrists, the rolls holding their shape, showing
the paler lining inside. Three wide silver reflective bands: one across the chest, one around each
sleeve below the elbow, and one over each shoulder. A vertical zip placket, a flap pocket on the
chest, a velcro tab. The yellow is bright and clearly yellow, not orange. The fabric is grubby,
faded unevenly, dirty at the hem and cuffs. Not a denim jacket, not soft canvas, not fitted, not
tailored.

UNDER THE JACKET
A soft pale green t-shirt with a faded cracked cartoon graphic on the chest, worn almost
illegible. Thin, washed out.

TIED AT THE WAIST
A warm burnt-orange sweatshirt, a rich terracotta orange, noticeably darker and redder than the
yellow jacket above it, tied by its sleeves, the two sleeves knotted together in a thick twist at
the front. The body of the sweatshirt is short and bunched, hanging only a little way down, not
reaching his thighs. Faded, grubby. It is a knotted sweatshirt, never a skirt.

HANGING AT HIS WAIST
A short chain clipped at his waist with three small worn keychain charms on it: a small red
plastic tag, a round yellow enamel disc, a tiny grey plastic gadget. Scuffed and faded.

TROUSERS
Baggy olive-khaki cropped trousers, loose through the leg, gathered into ribbed cuffs that stop
below the knee. Large flap pockets on the thighs. Worn, creased, slightly stained.

SOCKS — TWO DIFFERENT SOCKS, DELIBERATELY MISMATCHED
He is wearing one sock of each of two different designs. Both are thick ribbed white athletic
socks pulled to mid-calf.
The sock on his ORANGE foot has two bands around the top, one orange and one red.
The sock on his GREEN foot has two bands around the top, both green.
The two socks are never the same as each other in any view. In the front view the orange-banded
sock is on the figure's left leg as we see it; in the reverse view the sides swap, so the
orange-banded sock appears on the opposite side of the frame. The two socks also sit at slightly
different heights, one pulled higher than the other.

SHOES — WORN IN BOTH FULL LENGTH VIEWS
Grey and off-white worn running trainers on both feet, chunky retro shape, scuffed and dirty,
grubby mesh panels, soles worn unevenly.

VIEW 1 — FULL LENGTH FRONT, LEFT THIRD OF THE SHEET
Head to shoes, whole figure in frame with clearance above the helmet and below the shoes. Camera
at waist height, lens axis perfectly horizontal and level, verticals parallel, no distortion.

VIEW 2 — FULL LENGTH REVERSE, MIDDLE THIRD OF THE SHEET
The same figure photographed from the opposite side of the studio, same distance, same camera
height, same framing. This view exists to show the reverse of the garments: the rear of the helmet
with its stickers and scuffs, the hair escaping below the helmet rim, the wide reflective band
across the shoulder blades of the jacket, the knotted sweatshirt, the cropped trousers and the
trainers.

VIEW 3 — TIGHT HEAD SHOT, RIGHT THIRD OF THE SHEET
A tight head shot, straight on, filling the whole of the remaining third of the sheet, top to
bottom, much larger in scale than the two full length views. He is wearing the helmet. The helmet,
its stickers, cracks and rusted rivets, the frayed navy chin strap, the short tufts of hair
escaping around the helmet rim, his protruding ears, the scratched glasses and his face all
rendered in sharp detail. Skin texture fully visible — pores, moles, faint shine.

LIGHT
Neutral, soft, even studio lighting for all three views. Large soft source from above and slightly
to the front, white bounce fill on the shadow side. No colour cast, no dramatic shadows, no rim
light. Full contact shadow beneath his shoes in the two full length views.

TEXTURE
Photoreal materials — crazed helmet paint, frayed webbing, stiff technical uniform fabric, scuffed
soft leather, thin cotton jersey, fleece, scuffed mesh. Fine organic film grain. Neutral accurate

105mm at f8 for the full length views, lens axis level, no distortion, whole figure sharp.

Photoreal 16:9 film still from a Japanese feature on 35mm. No captions or watermarks.

STYLE: Japanese and Hong Kong cinema, late nineties -- olive-green city, saturated colour.

THE MOMENT: Rush hour has stopped on a wide one-way Tokyo avenue, humid summer evening.

COMPOSITION -- off-centre: The camera stands left of the centreline and turns a few degrees right, the avenue running away diagonally, the vanishing point far right of centre. The left buildings take more width than the right. The camera sits low, barely above bonnet height: the nearest taxis loom in the bottom corners, cropped by the lower edge, one windscreen showing its driver.

DEPTH AND HAZE -- graded by distance: The humid haze is not uniform. In the foreground and middle ground the air is clear and colour full; haze begins only beyond the middle of the street and thickens into the distance, where buildings pale to cream. Nothing near or mid-frame is washed out.

SATURATION: The nearest and middle signboards and vehicles hold full colour -- scarlet, mustard-gold, jade-green, cobalt, crimson, deep and undiluted. Only the far distance desaturates. Colour is strongest at the bottom and centre.

LIGHT -- sun just below the rooftops: The sky is blown to pale warm cream. Where the silhouettes meet it, a burning amber-orange line ignites along every roofline and antenna. The topmost floors of the tallest blocks catch the last raking gold; everything lower has dropped into shade.

THE LIGHTS -- festive: The street is alight. Neon boards switched on down both sides, glowing from within in scarlet, amber, white, jade-green and deep blue, a dense constellation into the distance. Shop windows spill warm light on the pavement. Every taxi carries a lit roof lamp, reflecting in windscreens and wet asphalt.

THE HEADLAMPS: Every car has its lights switched on. Twin lamps burn white on each front -- the glass blown to pure clipped white at the centre, a warm amber rim around it, each throwing a soft halo into the air. The nearest flare brightest into wide glowing discs; those behind shrink to hot white points running deep into the distance. Each pair drags a vertical smear of white light down the damp asphalt.

VALUES, brightest to darkest: the headlamps, the blown sky and lit signs; the pale facades; the asphalt, darker than the buildings; the shadowed flanks of the cars.

THE GREEN: The olive-green cast runs through the whole depth of the picture, not only the upper facades -- in the concrete, the shaded shopfronts, the lower half of the frame. Dusty dark-green trees line both pavements, a cluster close on the left. The asphalt still catches a warm amber bounce.

THE TRAFFIC -- one-way, gridlocked, varied: Every vehicle faces the same direction, nose-on toward camera, four dense lanes, no oncoming lane. No two alike. Boxy period Japanese taxis in crimson, mustard-gold, cream-and-red, deep green and dull silver, among them a white box truck, a cream minivan, a kei van. The roofline rises and falls where vans break the rows of cars.

THE SIGNBOARD CRUSH: Along the whole left edge the boards pile up -- overlapping, layered, jutting at different angles and heights, no bare wall between. Tall narrow strips, many times taller than wide, dense with columns of bold characters.

THE BUILDINGS: Pale olive-grey concrete and tile, light in value. Heights jostle: a two-storey shopfront beside a ten-storey block beside a narrow tower.

CAMERA & LENS: Arriflex 535B on a vintage uncoated telephoto prime, wide open, light black diffusion. The nearest cars stay sharp; beyond, the street falls into soft film blur.

GRADE: Warmth is confined to the sky, the signs, the taxi bodywork and the foreground road. Everything else is olive khaki-green, faintly cool, never golden, never neutral, never blue. No black in the metal -- the darkest tone is saturated russet-brown. Blacks lifted. Fine 35mm grain.

FEELING: A city holding its breath in the heat, going nowhere, lit like a carnival.

Boxy period Japanese taxis in crimson, mustard-gold, cream-and-red, deep green and dull silver. Among them a white box truck, a cream minivan, a kei van, a low compact. Tall narrow vertical strips, many times taller than wide, each dense with lettering: a column of large bold Japanese characters running top to bottom, filling the panel. Backgrounds of black-blue navy with pale characters, greenish-white with dark, deep red with white.

Different heights jostle: a squat two-storey shopfront beside a ten-storey block beside a narrow tower, ragged setbacks and gaps of sky. A distant expressway crosses the street. Dusty dark-green trees line both pavements, a cluster close on the left.

A small old shokudo that happens to serve pizza, decorated over thirty years by one family. The
walls are split: pale warm white plaster above, and below waist height a band of dark varnished
timber panelling with a strip of faded orange painted along it.

THE WALLS — A JAPANESE IZAKAYA-STYLE PIZZA SHOP, EVERY OBJECT SHARP AND SPECIFIC: everything above
the panelling is covered, and every single item on the wall is rendered crisply and precisely, a
real object with real edges, never vague, never smeared, never approximate. Tall handwritten
tanzaku menu strips in Japanese brushed in black ink on butter-yellow paper with red price figures,
taped up in uneven columns. A large old advertising poster for beer or ramen, faded and
sun-bleached, its Japanese lettering still legible in shape. A framed certificate of merit hung
proudly in the middle of the wall, an award for the shop's pizza, its border printed and its seal
red. Old framed family photographs in mismatched frames. Small enamel advertising tin signs. A wall
calendar with a kanji masthead. A framed black and white picture of the shop on its opening day. A
single red daruma doll with one eye filled in, sitting on a small shelf among the frames. Along the
very top of the wall, where it meets the ceiling, a continuous row of small old enamel plates and
signs pinned edge to edge like a border. Nothing lines up with anything else — it has all been
added one piece at a time over decades and never rearranged.

TWO RED PAPER LANTERNS, SWITCHED ON: two round red paper akachochin hang low from the ceiling over
the counter, lit from within, glowing a deep warm red through their ribbed paper. They throw a soft
red-amber wash down onto the counter top and out into the room, faint but clearly present, tinting
the surfaces nearest them and lifting the shadows a little. They are gentle, never bright, always
quieter than the sunlight — a second, warmer layer of light beneath the golden band.

Japanese through and through: a small wooden kamidana shrine shelf high in the corner with a fresh
offering cup and a paper streamer. A maneki-neko with one paw up beside the till. A chipped mug of
chopsticks and a tissue box in a plastic holder on the counter. Plastic beer crates stacked in a
corner.

Small signs of a family that lives here: a child's crayon drawing taped up among the photographs. A
tiny potted plant on the end of the counter, surviving. A folded newspaper and a pair of reading
glasses left on a stool where someone got up mid-sentence. A row of small ornaments and lucky
charms accumulated along a shelf. Nothing arranged, all of it just where it was put.

The far wall, around the oven: a single plain wooden shelf running along it at head height with a
row of storage tins and a couple of jars, and beneath it a short rail of hanging tools — a
long-handled pizza peel, a brush, a pair of tongs. A stack of pizza trays leaning against the wall
beside the oven.

The counter stands in the middle of the room and splits it in two along its length. On its left
side, the customer side, a row of mismatched plastic stools pulled up to it. On its right side,
behind it, the working side of the shop. The pizza oven is set into the far wall straight ahead, on
the working side, fired, its mouth a low ellipse of ember orange.

THE DOORWAY ON THE RIGHT — LONGER NOREN: a plain wooden door frame with a noren curtain hanging in
it, and that curtain reaches halfway down the opening — a good deal longer than a short shop noren,
falling to roughly waist height rather than stopping at head height. Split into vertical panels
with straight-cut edges, the cloth soft and faded, the panels parted a little in the middle.

The last low sun comes almost horizontally through venetian blinds on the left and cuts a hard
golden band diagonally across the room, the slat bars sharp and defined, dust turning in the beam.
Where it lands, surfaces burn bright. It is by far the strongest light in the picture. Away from
it the room falls into deep shadow, warmed only by the red lantern glow and the mouth of the oven.

Camera low, tucked into a corner, looking diagonally down the length of the room along the counter.
Nothing centred, nothing symmetrical.

THE RIDER IS A GIANT STRONGMAN. Enormous, far bigger than any ordinary man — but built, not soft: a heavyweight wrestler's body, real slabs of muscle under a covering layer of fat. Nothing about him is flabby or sagging.

THE MACHINE IS TINY — IT IS A CHILD'S QUAD BIKE: a small youth-sized all-terrain quad, the kind built for a twelve-year-old. Its wheels would come no higher than a grown man's knee. Its handlebars are no wider than a child's shoulders. Its whole length from bumper to tail is less than the height of an ordinary adult. It is a small machine in absolute terms, not a large machine seen next to a large man.

AND HE IS HEAPED ON TOP OF IT: perched high above it, easily twice its height sitting down, his body far wider than its bodywork and overhanging it on every side. His knees are folded right up toward his chest, higher than the handlebars. His huge fists swallow the little grips and almost touch each other, his elbows sticking far out. The seat has disappeared completely beneath him. His feet are far too big for the small footwells, crammed in and spilling over their edges, but nothing of him touches the ground — the machine carries all of him. Its suspension is fully compressed under his weight and its small tyres are flattened and bulging.

THE MACHINE IS ORANGE: faded industrial safety orange across the fenders and bodywork, sun-bleached, chalked and dusty, scraped and dented, patched with mismatched sheet, riveted and wired back together, rust blooming from every seam, a few sheltered corners still holding the gloss it once had. Four fat little balloon tyres with deep knobbly tread, short-travel suspension, a narrow straddle seat, small sculpted fenders, shallow footwells, a small tubular rack at the back.

HE IS ARMOURED LIKE A FIGHTER, IN DARK PIECES OVER BARE SKIN: heavy protectors of near-black moulded rubber and blackened boiled leather, scarred and scuffed, buckled on with worn straps — thick cupped elbow guards, broad knee guards, and wide bracers wrapped around both forearms from wrist to elbow. They are the darkest things he wears and sit in strong contrast against the pale bare skin around them.

ON EACH SHOULDER, a thick pad cut from car tyre with a much coarser tread than the little wheels below, and driven up through each pad from underneath, a cluster of long crude rebar spikes — rusted, uneven in length and angle, roughly cut at the tips, standing clearly proud above the rubber, present and unmistakable on both shoulders.

THE FUEL DRUM: a battered translucent drum strapped to the front of the machine, clearly visible and unobstructed, holding a thick milky opaque phosphor liquid — cloudy, pale, a soft muted yellow-green — glowing gently from within as a diffused luminous mass rather than shining like a lamp. It is large on this small machine. A corrugated hose runs up from it to the filter fitting at his chin.

THE EXHAUST IS PLAINLY VISIBLE: a heavy rusted pipe rising up and back from the rear, standing clear of the bodywork against the grey behind it, its mouth open and blackened with soot, unmistakable in this side view and never hidden behind him. No flame, no smoke.

A SAFARI LIGHT BAR ACROSS THE FRONT: a crude scaffold of pipe bolted above the little bonnet carrying six or seven round spotlights, all different sizes and makes, mismatched and salvaged — some in dented chrome bowls, some in painted housings, one cracked, one bound on with tape and wire, all switched on and blazing bright warm white straight ahead. The bar is comically oversized for the machine it is bolted to.

A BRIGHT BANNER AT HIS WAIST: tied at one hip and hanging over that thigh, a large piece cut from an old Japanese advertising banner — thick printed vinyl, sun-worn but still strongly coloured, its big cartoon face and broken Japanese characters plainly readable, cracked along its folds, frayed at the edges. The motorcycle is homemade, welded from mismatched scrap tubing of different diameters, with no bodywork at all and the engine completely exposed. Its frame is roughly brush-painted in vermilion red-orange lead primer, chipped and flaking away to rust underneath. Behind the seat the tail of the machine rises steeply upward into a tall backrest that sweeps up and back well above the rider's waist — one single solid piece of steel plate, cut from sheet with a torch and bent into a long upswept shape, welded straight onto the frame with a thick untidy bead of weld along the join, its cut edges rough and uneven, the whole panel rusted and streaked. One flat continuous slab, not an assembly of bars. The fuel tank sits high inside the frame triangle directly below the handlebars, cradled between the tubes where a normal tank would sit, strapped in place with mismatched clips and wire and clearly visible in the open frame — a battered half translucent vessel holding a thick milky opaque phosphor liquid, cloudy and pale, a soft muted yellow-green, glowing gently from within as a diffused luminous mass rather than shining like a lamp. A long corrugated rubber hose runs up from that tank to the rider's mask. At the back a crude exhaust pipe, welded from mismatched sections and rusted along its length, is going off like a furnace: a long torch of flame beats out of its mouth — pale and almost neutral in colour, no brighter than the headlamp, tinted faintly with the same phosphor green and with a little dirty yellow low down where the flame leaves the metal — and behind it a huge churning column of smoke pours out in that same pale phosphor green, thick and rolling, boiling out across the frame behind the machine, thinning only at its far edges. At the front a single large round headlamp, oversized and battered in a rusted rim, burns bright and neutral white with the faintest green cast of that same phosphor in it.

The rider is an extremely tall, gaunt, wiry man: enormously long-limbed and rangy, all cord and sinew with no bulk at all, ribs and hip bones showing, shoulder blades standing out, tendons standing in his neck and forearms, so much too long for the machine that his knees ride up near his elbows and he folds over it like a spider. His torso is completely bare — weathered, thick with old scars, with the remains of a faded traditional Japanese tattoo across his ribs, cut through and ruined by the scarring.

Tied around his waist and hanging down over his hips and thighs like a heavy apron is a large piece cut from an old Japanese advertising banner — thick printed vinyl, sun-worn but still clearly colourful. The printing on it is huge: the smiling face of a cartoon manga girl, or a cartoon kitten, filling most of the hanging panel and instantly recognisable, drawn in the flat cheerful style of a shopfront advert. It is printed on a warm cream ground in terracotta and brick red, with one accent of deep signboard green and a line of dusty gold. Two or three enormous Japanese characters run across it, most of them broken and cut off by the folds, the knot and the torn edges, so only fragments of each survive. The vinyl is cracked along every fold line, its edges frayed, grommet holes torn out along one side, grimed black in the creases, and it is stiff — it bends in hard flat planes and stands away from his legs rather than draping.

He wears trousers built from scavenged parts: riveted steel plates painted the same chipped vermilion over thick leather and torn military webbing, mismatched buckles, everything patched and mended. On each shoulder sits a thick epaulette built up from stacked slabs of cut car tyre, the tread still visible and the rubber cracked and perished at the edges — and driven straight through each rubber pad, from underneath and out through the top, are long crude rebar spikes, jutting up and outward at uneven angles and lengths, their ends rusted and roughly cut. The rubber is the pad; the spikes come out of it.

His entire head is sealed inside a full-head rusted gas mask: a heavy riveted steel and blackened rubber hood covering the whole skull front, back, top and sides, down to the collarbones, with no opening anywhere. Tied around his waist and hanging down over his hips and thighs like a heavy apron is a large piece cut from an old Japanese advertising banner — thick printed vinyl, sun-worn but still clearly colourful. The printing on it is huge: the smiling face of a cartoon manga girl, or a cartoon kitten, filling most of the hanging panel and instantly recognisable, drawn in the flat cheerful style of a shopfront advert. It is printed on a warm cream ground in terracotta and brick red, with one accent of deep signboard green and a line of dusty gold. Two or three enormous Japanese characters run across it, most of them broken and cut off by the folds, the knot and the torn edges, so only fragments of each survive. The vinyl is cracked along every fold line, its edges frayed, grommet holes torn out along one side, grimed black in the creases, and it is stiff — it bends in hard flat planes and stands away from his legs rather than draping.

He wears trousers built from scavenged parts: riveted steel plates painted the same chipped vermilion over thick leather and torn military webbing, mismatched buckles, everything patched and mended. On each shoulder sits a thick epaulette built up from stacked slabs of cut car tyre, and driven straight through each rubber pad from underneath are long crude rebar spikes, jutting up and outward at uneven angles and lengths. Every one of those spikes is alight: a flame burns at each rusted tip in the same pale phosphor green as the exhausts, and a ribbon of the same pale green smoke lifts from each one, so his shoulders carry two small crowns of fire of their own.

His entire head is sealed inside a full-head rusted gas mask: a heavy riveted steel and blackened rubber hood covering the whole skull front, back, top and sides, down to the collarbones, with no opening anywhere. Bolted along the crown of the mask, running front to back, is a tall savage mohawk crest — not hair but a dense brush of frayed steel wire rope, the strands sprung open and splayed stiffly upward like bristles, rusted and oil-blackened, with a few tarred rope dreadlocks hanging down from the back of it.

No flame and no smoke ever crosses the mask, the crest or the printed banner — those stay clear and fully readable through all of it.

Everything else is rust, oil-black, dead leather and grey perished rubber. The whole picture is held to a narrow warm palette — cream, terracotta, brick red, dusty gold, deep green, rust and black — with the pale phosphor green of the fuel, the flames, the smoke and the headlamp as the only cold note in it.

Wide side-on tracking shot of a motorised bed driving down a Tokyo street at night, early 2000s, whole vehicle in profile end to end, nothing cropped. A metal folding camp bed, thin mattress made up with a cream and red striped cotton bedsheet, its loose edge untucked and hanging down over the sides of the mattress in soft crumpled folds, head end propped into a low backrest, on four fat chromed motorcycle wheels, frame reinforced with welded steel tube, a car battery bungeed on, taped cables, a bicycle bell. Two long chromed exhaust pipes run horizontally along the lower side rail, the bed's whole length front to back, exiting behind the backrest, tips angled up and out, one wrapped in flaking heat tape, trailing smoke. Propped behind his back, a big plush cushion shaped like a domed toadstool cap, red with round white spots, squashed under his shoulders. Clamped to the backrest, a retro desk lamp on a jointed spring arm, dented cream shade, craning over his shoulder, pouring warm orange light onto him.
THE TELEVISION SITS AT THE HEAD END ONLY. A boxy CRT television is bolted to a bracket rising above and behind the backrest, higher than the top of his head, well behind his shoulders. Its bare back panel and cooling vents face him; the screen is turned the other way, facing rearward down the street behind the bed, showing grey static and rolling interference to the road it has already passed, casting cold flicker onto the exhaust tips and the smoke trailing behind. A grey console taped to the frame beneath it.
THE FOOT END CARRIES ONLY A HEADLAMP. A single round headlamp is mounted low at the foot of the bed, throwing a beam forward down the street. Beyond that the foot end is bare frame and open mattress with his crossed ankles resting on it - no screen, no cabinet, no monitor, no second television anywhere in the lower half of the frame.
Reclining against the backrest, half lying down, a heavyset unshaven Japanese man of about forty, legs stretched flat along the mattress, ankles crossed, fuzzy striped knitted slippers in orange and pink pulled on over slightly grubby white socks. An opened bag of potato chips lies torn along one side beside his hip, a few crisps spilled onto the sheet. He holds a grey plastic controller out in both hands like a steering wheel, arms extended forward: a trident-shaped pad, three prongs, central grip with a thumbstick, black cross pad left, four coloured buttons right. Very broad and soft, a heavy round belly, thick neck, full jowly cheeks, a wide flat nose, patchy black stubble across the jaw and above the lip. His mouth is closed with the lower lip pushed slightly forward, chin tucked, an idle unbothered look aimed far ahead. A sheen of sweat on his forehead and chest catching the lamplight. Thick black shaggy hair in a loose home perm, tight frizzy curls bunching out from under the cap and hanging down over both ears to the jawline, sideburns merging into the stubble, the crown flattened where the cap presses. A low-crown five-panel baseball cap, bright red with a plain white front panel and a red brim, worn straight and pushed back a little, no logo and no lettering. Narrow wraparound sport sunglasses, glossy black plastic frames with dark curved lenses hugging the temples, small oval lenses sitting close to the eyes, hard specular glints of neon on the glass. A loose open short-sleeve camp shirt in cream printed with a dense muted botanical pattern of soft olive, tan and faded rust leaves and blossoms, boxy cut, worn fully unbuttoned and hanging open off both shoulders, the panels pushed aside so his bare chest and belly are exposed down the middle, collar splayed flat, fabric limp and crumpled. A thin black headset, earpiece over one ear, boom mic at his mouth.
Baggy 1990s motocross racing trousers in heavy nylon and canvas, cut wide and loose over the legs, gathered at the ankle. Bold graphic colour blocking in big flat panels: acid yellow-green, deep teal, scarlet red, pale ice blue and charcoal grey, split by broad diagonal bands and chevrons sweeping across thigh and knee, edged with contrast piping. Padded knee panels, a flapped side pocket, a heavy webbing waist strap with a metal buckle. Entirely blank - geometric decoration only, no letters, words, numbers or logos. Scuffed and creased.
Beyond, a shopping street dissolving into coloured bokeh: vertical neon in red, green, magenta, overhead cables, a konbini glow, wet asphalt. Сделай прическу чтобы: PONYTAILS - two enormous short ponytails high on the crown, sitting directly side by side and touching, no gap between them. All the hair on the head goes into these two, so each contains half a head of hair.

THICKNESS - each ponytail is huge and solid: the bound base is as thick as the wearer's forearm, and the mass above it is thicker still, wider than it is long. No gaps, nothing you can see through.

LENGTH - SHORT. Each ponytail is only about as long as the face is tall, from hairline to chin. It rises above the crown and stops. It does not arc over, does not curve down past the ears, and does not reach the shoulders. Short and stubby relative to its enormous thickness.

DENSITY GRADIENT - the base and the body of each ponytail are packed dense and solid. Toward the tip the mass loosens and opens: the hair separates into thinner, sparser strands that splay apart and let the background show between them, so each ponytail is heavy and opaque at the bottom and thin, wispy and broken up at the very top.

BASE WRAP - a very wide band of hair is coiled around each base, wrapped several turns so it forms a broad thick collar, as tall as a thumb, completely hiding the elastic.

COLOUR - mostly red hair, with a few narrow ribbons of scarlet, magenta and turquoise running up through the mass.

FRINGE - a sparse wispy red fringe of fine separated strands over the forehead.

FOUR PHOTOGRAPHS FROM ONE STUDIO SESSION, documenting a practical creature build for a feature film — a real actor in silicone prosthetics, hand-punched hair and resin horns, photographed on a stage. Full-frame camera, 50mm prime at f5.6, ISO 200.

THE LIGHT IS DARK AND HARD: a single softbox high and well to camera-left, close in, falling off fast, so the shadow side of the figure sinks deep. Only a weak bounce card low right, just enough to keep the dark side from going empty — shadows stay deep and readable, never crushed to black. A bare head behind camera-right lays a hard bright rim down one edge of the figure. A low key image with brilliant colour inside it: the darkness is in the lighting, never in the paint.

LAYOUT: one wide image holding FOUR views of the SAME character, evenly spaced left to right on one flat background, identical costume, proportions and lighting in every view: (1) full-body FRONT, facing camera, (2) full-body SIDE PROFILE, (3) full-body BACK, (4) a large tight CLOSE-UP of head and shoulders on the right. Arms hanging relaxed at the sides, weight even, feet apart.

THE FIGURE: a lean, wiry, middle-aged man, narrow through the shoulders and hips, standing barefoot.

THE FACE: European bone structure — a long straight nose with a slight bump at the bridge, high flat cheekbones, a squared jaw, deep-set eyes under a heavy brow ridge, and a strikingly high, broad, bare forehead, the hairline set far back so the whole upper face is open. Two deep vertical furrows stand between the brows and three horizontal creases cross the forehead, worn in permanently. Heavy black eyebrows. The ears are long and pointed, standing away from the head, tapering to a fine tip, the skin thin enough at the edge that the rim light glows dull orange-red through it.

THE GAZE — THIS IS THE PORTRAIT: the eyes are amber-yellow, the iris fibrous and streaked, ringed by a dark limbal edge, the pupil round and black and small. The chin is dropped a little and the head tilted barely forward, so he looks out from under the brow ridge and the eyes sit in shadow with only the yellow catching light. The lids are heavy and half-lowered. He is not snarling and not straining — the face is completely still, the stare fixed, level and unblinking, held far too long. The stillness of something that already knows how this ends. The fixed, weighted glare of a kabuki actor holding a mie.

THE SKIN — THE HEART OF THE IMAGE: brick red, the colour of fired clay, and it is not smooth. The whole surface is a dried crust, broken into a fine irregular crazing of hairline fissures like a mud flat after drought — dense and small across the cheeks, temples and the broad forehead, opening into wider splits down the sides of the neck, across the chest, over the backs of the hands and the tops of the feet. On the face these cracks are dark and dry, nothing more than deep lines. On the throat, the upper chest, the hands and the feet they run molten: a fierce orange-yellow glow deep inside them, brightest at the centre of each split and fading along its length, burning hard enough in this low light to throw its own warm glow up under the jaw and onto the inside of the collar.

The red is not one flat colour. It runs deeper and browner in the hollows — under the cheekbones, around the eye sockets, in the crease of the neck — and rises paler and pinker on the raised planes of the forehead, nose and cheekbones where the crust is thinnest and stretched. Between the cracks the surface carries fine open pores, larger and stretched around the nose, invisible on the eyelids.

The sheen is uneven and physical: a slick oily shine down the nose, on the inner brow and the point of the chin, catching the softbox as a bright irregular smear; the cheeks dry and matte; a flaking, lifting patch of crust beside one nostril and along the outer jaw. Nothing is symmetrical — one eyelid heavier, one nostril fractionally wider, the crazing denser on one side of the face than the other, one old healed split running back from the corner of the mouth.

THE TUSKS: two long ivory tusks growing from under the upper lip, one each side, curving outward and sweeping up in a smooth arc past the cheeks, their tips ending clear of the cheekbones. They must grow from beneath the lip and never from the cheeks. Aged ivory, warm cream at the root and paler toward the tip, faintly translucent where the light passes through the last few centimetres, the surface bearing fine lengthwise growth lines, a few shallow scratches and a chip on one. The left edge of the carriageway is a clean, straight, unbroken line: a neat concrete kerb running the entire length, its edge crisp and even, with the painted chequer reaching right up to it and never stopping short. The carriageway is exactly the same width everywhere. No crumbled kerb, no broken-off slabs, no missing asphalt, no bites taken out of the deck, no exposed reinforcing bar, no rubble, no debris on the road. The surface is worn and filthy with age, as everywhere in this world, but structurally perfect.

Every post is still standing and still attached to it. The surface is worn and filthy with age, as everywhere in this world, but structurally perfect. Everything that is destroyed sits ON that intact edge, bolted to it — the guardrail and nothing else.

Its face is matte black glass, absolutely dark, set in a rusted steel casing.
Across the upper part of each board, three hazard symbols in a row: three triangles, each with a thick exclamation mark inside it, drawn in fine dense red dots — the dots small and closely packed, hundreds of them, each an individual pinpoint of hot bright red burning against the black. The whole surface is marked exactly as a Japanese expressway is marked, but the markings intensify
wherever the road is dangerous.

turns. Worn thin in the wheel tracks, patched in places, the edges ragged.

hatch fill the concrete between the diverging lanes — long parallel white stripes at an angle,
covering whole wedges of road, packed close. The hatching gets denser as the divergence narrows.

across the lanes, one set after another down the road, pointing forward. Standard Japanese highway
arrows, worn and repainted.

tightly spaced, the spacing closing up as the corner nears.

Cat's eyes: small reflective studs set into the lane lines, catching the light in chains of tiny
points running away down every road at every level.

WHAT THIS PLACE IS: a cheerful, well-kept Japanese neighbourhood pizza izakaya that has been open
for thirty years and is loved by its street. Bright, tidy, welcoming, full of colour. Not gloomy,
not abandoned, not derelict, not a sad forgotten place — somebody has just stepped out of the room
and will be back in a moment.

THE LAYOUT — HOLD THIS EXACTLY
The doorway through to the back kitchen is on the RIGHT-HAND SIDE WALL — not on the far wall, not
beside the oven. A plain wooden door frame with a proper traditional cloth noren hanging in it,
reaching about halfway down the opening to roughly waist height, split into vertical panels, the
panels parted a little in the middle. Through that gap, out of focus: the back kitchen, its walls a
deep forest green, a stainless steel prep table, steel shelves — a cool green room glimpsed from
this warm one.
Directly opposite it, on the LEFT-HAND SIDE WALL, a long horizontal window running most of the
length of that wall, with old venetian blinds across it.
On the FAR WALL straight ahead, between the two, the pizza oven: a squat domed oven set into the
wall, fired, its mouth a low ellipse of ember orange. The oven and the doorway are on different
walls, well apart from each other.
The counter is a single plain straight run down the middle of the room, splitting it in two along
its length — no bends, no corners, no L-shape. Its left side is the customer side, a row of
mismatched plastic stools pulled up to it; behind it on the right, the working side of the shop.

THE WALLS
Above waist height, clean pale cream plaster. Below it, all the way round the room, a bright warm
orange painted band — vivid, cheerful, freshly kept, smooth painted plaster with no timber, no
panelling, no wood grain. The orange is a strong happy colour, not a faded stain.

THE WALL DRESSING — EVERY OBJECT DELIBERATE, SPECIFIC AND SHARPLY DRAWN
The cream plaster above the orange band is covered, and every single item is a real object with
real edges, drawn precisely, never vague, never smeared, never approximate:
tall handwritten tanzaku menu slips brushed in black ink on butter-yellow paper with red price
figures, taped up in uneven columns;
a large advertising poster for beer or ramen, its Japanese lettering crisp in shape;
a framed certificate of merit hung with pride in the middle of the wall — an award for the shop's
pizza, printed border, red seal;
old framed family photographs in mismatched frames;
small enamel advertising tin signs;
a wall calendar with a kanji masthead;
a framed black and white photograph of the shop on its opening day;
one red daruma doll with a single eye filled in, on a small shelf among the frames;
a kamidana shrine shelf high in the corner with a fresh offering cup and a paper streamer;
a maneki-neko with one paw up beside the till;
along the very top of the wall, a continuous row of small enamel plates and signs pinned edge to
edge like a border.
Nothing lines up with anything else — added one piece at a time over decades — but nothing is
careless, and every item is legible as an object.

TWO RED PAPER LANTERNS, SWITCHED ON: two round red paper akachochin hang over the counter, lit from
within, glowing a rich warm red through their ribbed paper and adding their colour to the room.

THE LIGHT — WARM, LOW, GENEROUS, FILLING THE ROOM: the sun is very low outside and pours in almost
horizontally through the long venetian blinds on the left. Its light is deep golden-orange, the
colour of the last hour of the day, and it does not merely cut a band — it floods the whole
interior, striping the room with slat bars while filling every corner with warm bounced light off
the cream walls and the orange band. The room is bright and glowing throughout. Shadows are present
and soft, warm and open, never black, never heavy, never gloomy. Air full of turning dust, lit gold.
The whole picture is warm, sunny and inviting.

THE FEEL: clean and cheerful. Surfaces wiped, floor swept, crates stacked neatly, a chipped mug of
chopsticks and a tissue box in a plastic holder on the counter. A heavy old cream cash register and
a squat late-1990s landline telephone at the customer end. A child's crayon drawing taped up among
the photographs, a small potted plant on the end of the counter, a folded newspaper and reading
glasses left on a stool where someone got up mid-sentence. Old and worn but bright and cared for.

The far wall, around the oven: a plain wooden shelf at head height with storage tins and jars, and
beneath it a short rail of hanging tools — a long-handled pizza peel, a brush, a pair of tongs. A

mid-sentence. Nothing arranged, all of it just where it was put.

small opening with a short noren curtain hanging in it.

FOCUS, THE DEFINING CHOICE: extremely shallow depth of field, almost the entire frame out of focus. The single sharp plane sits a few metres beyond: the illuminated roof-light box on a taxi three cars ahead, the only detail that resolves. Everything past it collapses again, the queue and the street dissolving into soft stacked masses and round glowing discs.
CAMERA HEIGHT: we are inside the traffic, not above it. The lens sits at 1.3 metres, level with the roofs of the nearest cars. Not elevated, no view from above, no plan view of the asphalt. It tilts up so the buildings lean over us.
